title: The graph with too many boxes
scenario: A market-intelligence team wants an AI system that writes a weekly competitor report. Each week the list of competitors and the sources worth checking change. Some requests are quick facts, others are full reports. A colleague drew the first design (exhibit). You review it before anyone builds it. The company and the design are made up for this case.
exhibit:
PROPOSED DESIGN (made up for this case)

request
  -> lead agent decides freely: quick fact or full report
  -> research step: 5 fixed steps, always the same
       1 search news   2 search filings   3 search blogs
       4 search pricing pages   5 search job ads
  -> writer agent drafts the report
  -> report sent to 40 people

NOTES FROM THE REVIEW MEETING
- Some weeks only 2 of the 5 searches matter; other weeks a new source type is needed.
- Sales wants every report checked against a 6-point style rubric before it goes out.
- Finance wants quick-fact requests to always take the cheap path, every time.
- The full-report step must still choose its own searches each week.

questions.prompt: The research subtasks change from week to week. Which pattern from Anthropic's post fits the research step best?

options.text: Prompt chaining: keep the five fixed search steps, in the same order.
options.explanation: Anthropic says prompt chaining suits tasks that split cleanly into fixed subtasks. Here the subtasks change each week.

options.text: Routing: classify each request and send it down one fixed path.
options.explanation: Routing picks one specialized follow-up per input category. It does not decide a new set of subtasks for each request.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: an LLM picks the subtasks from each input.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic: in orchestrator-workers, subtasks are not pre-defined but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input.

options.text: Voting: run the same five searches several times and compare.
options.explanation: Voting runs the same task several times for diverse outputs. It does not solve the problem that the needed searches change.

questions.prompt: Sales wants each report checked against a 6-point rubric and improved until it passes. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one call writes, another grades it and sends feedback.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says this pattern works well when there are clear evaluation criteria and refinement adds value. A fixed rubric is a clear criterion.

options.text: Routing: send each report to one of six rubric agents, then publish.
options.explanation: Routing sends an input to one path. The rubric needs every report checked and then improved, not sorted.

options.text: Sectioning: split the report into six parts and write each part in parallel.
options.explanation: Sectioning splits work into independent subtasks. It does not add a check-and-improve loop.

options.text: Add the rubric to the writer's prompt and send the first draft.
options.explanation: This adds no check at all. Nothing confirms the draft passes before it goes to 40 people.

questions.prompt: Finance wants quick-fact requests to take the cheap path every time. How should the first step decide?

options.text: Keep the lead agent deciding freely, and prompt it to prefer the cheap path.
options.explanation: A prompt can push the model, but the choice is still made by the model each time. Finance asked for the same path every time.

options.text: Run both paths for every request and keep whichever answer costs less.
options.explanation: That pays for the expensive path on every request, which is the cost Finance wants to avoid.

options.text: Let every agent vote on the category and take the majority answer.
options.explanation: Voting adds more model calls and still leaves the path to model output. It does not make the flow decided by code.

options.text: Classify with a structured output, then let code pick the agent.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI Agents SDK docs list this as orchestrating via code, which makes tasks more deterministic and predictable in speed, cost and performance.

questions.prompt: Finance wants a fixed quick-fact path, and the report step must still adapt each week. How do the OpenAI docs suggest combining these?

options.text: One lead agent decides everything, including the path, from its prompt.
options.explanation: That is orchestrating via LLM only. Finance asked for a fixed path, which a prompt cannot guarantee.

options.text: Code fixes every step, including the five searches, so nothing varies.
options.explanation: That is orchestrating via code only. The searches would stay the same, but the needed sources change each week.

options.text: Code picks fact or report; a model picks the report's searches.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say you can mix and match: code decides the flow, and a model decides inside one step.

options.text: A model picks fact or report; code fixes the searches inside the report.
options.explanation: This reverses the roles. The path stays model-chosen, and the changing searches stay hard-coded.
